lesson.title: Decapsulation: Unwrapping the Boxes in Reverse Order
lesson.summary: Decapsulation is the receiving side's mirror image of encapsulation, stripping away one header and trailer at a time until only the original message remains.
lesson.body:
Every layer of wrapping added on the way out has to be removed on the way in, and it has to be removed in exactly the reverse order it was added. This process is called decapsulation. Where encapsulation builds up nested envelopes as a message travels down through the sending side's layers, decapsulation peels those envelopes back off as the same message travels up through the receiving side's layers, one header and trailer at a time, until the original content is recovered unchanged.

The order matters enormously, and it follows directly from how encapsulation stacked things up. Recall the earlier example: an HTTP message became the payload of a TCP segment, which became the payload of an IP packet, which became the payload of an Ethernet frame. On arrival, the receiving computer must undo that in the opposite sequence. First it strips the Ethernet header and trailer, checking the trailer's frame check sequence to confirm the frame was not corrupted before trusting anything inside it. What remains is handed up as an IP packet. Next it strips the IP header, using the protocol field inside that header to know the remaining payload should go to TCP. What remains is handed up as a TCP segment. Finally it strips the TCP header, using the port number inside it to know which specific application should receive what is left. What remains, at last, is the original HTTP message: "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1".

Each layer performing decapsulation only ever looks at the header, and trailer if present, that it itself understands. The Ethernet driver has no idea what a TCP port number is, and the web server has no idea what a hardware address is, yet together, layer by layer, they correctly deliver the message end to end. This is the same separation of concerns that made encapsulation useful in the first place, just running in the opposite direction. Software at each layer trusts that the layer below it has already validated and correctly identified what it is handing upward.

It is worth noticing that decapsulation is also where a trailer's real value shows up. A header can be read the instant it arrives, but the frame check sequence in an Ethernet trailer can only be verified once the entire frame, header and payload included, has been received and recalculated. If that check fails during decapsulation, the frame is dropped right there, at the very first layer, before any of its contents are passed further up, saving every higher layer the trouble of processing data that was already known to be damaged.

This symmetric pair, encapsulation going down and decapsulation going up, is the basic mechanical rhythm that every layered network architecture depends on, and it is exactly what makes the next concept, organizing protocols into layers in the first place, workable in practice rather than just in theory.
